title: Meal delivery and help with food when arthritis makes cooking hard (UK guide)
meta_title: Meal Delivery When Arthritis Makes Cooking Hard (UK)
meta_description: When arthritis makes cooking hard: meals on wheels, frozen meal delivery, online shopping, help from the council and eating well enough (UK).
excerpt: When arthritis makes cooking hard: meals on wheels, frozen meal delivery, online shopping, help from the council and eating well enough (UK).
direct_answer: If arthritis pain or fatigue makes shopping and cooking hard, you have options. Ask your council whether it offers or can arrange meals on wheels, look at frozen or chilled ready-meal delivery companies, and use supermarket online shopping with delivery. A council needs assessment can arrange help with preparing meals, and Attendance Allowance or PIP can help pay for it. Choose meals with protein and some fruit and vegetables, keep easy snacks in, and follow reheating instructions. See your GP if you are losing weight without trying or have gone off your food. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

content:
When your hands, hips or knees hurt, or you are worn out by the end of the day, cooking can become the job you skip. Missed meals make tiredness and weakness worse, so it is worth finding a way to get good food in.

This guide is for people with arthritis who struggle to shop or cook, and for family arranging help. If you still want to cook but need easier ways, see cooking with arthritis and kitchen adaptations first.

Your main options

Meals on wheels from the council

Some councils still run or arrange hot or frozen meal delivery. Ring your council’s adult social care team and ask what is available locally. You may need an assessment first.

Frozen and chilled meal delivery companies

Several national companies deliver frozen or chilled ready meals to your door, often with soft or smaller portions and options for special diets. Check whether the driver can put meals in your freezer for you, and whether packaging is easy to open.

Supermarket online shopping

Most supermarkets deliver. Some offer priority slots for people who are disabled or older. Prepared vegetables, ready-grated cheese, tinned fish and microwave rice save chopping and lifting.

Local and voluntary help

Lunch clubs, community cafés and volunteer schemes in some areas offer a meal and company. Your GP surgery’s social prescribing link worker can tell you what is near you.

Help from the council and benefits

  • A free needs assessment can lead to a carer coming in to help prepare meals.
  • Attendance Allowance (if you are over State Pension age) or PIP (if you are younger) is not means-tested and can help pay for meals or help. See Attendance Allowance.
  • An occupational therapist can suggest equipment, such as a perching stool or kettle tipper, that makes simple food possible.

Eating well enough

  • Aim for some protein at each meal, such as milk, eggs, fish, beans, meat or yoghurt, to help keep muscles strong.
  • Add fruit and vegetables where you can: frozen and tinned count.
  • Keep easy snacks in, such as yoghurts, cheese and crackers, and fruit.
  • Drink regularly through the day.

If you have little appetite, small meals often may be easier. See appetite loss.

Food safety

Follow the reheating instructions on the pack until food is steaming hot all the way through. Keep chilled meals in the fridge and use them by the use-by date. Store frozen meals in the freezer straight away.

When to see your GP

See your GP if you are losing weight without trying, your clothes or rings have become loose, you have gone off your food for more than a few weeks, or you have trouble swallowing. These can be signs of malnutrition or another problem that needs checking. If swallowing is the issue, see speech and swallowing.

Ask NHS 111 or your GP for same-day advice if you cannot keep food or drink down. Call 999 if someone is choking and cannot clear it, or is very drowsy and confused.

For carers and family

Check what is in the fridge and freezer when you visit, and whether meals are being eaten. Set up online shopping together, and ask the council for a carer’s assessment if you are doing a lot of the cooking.

Common questions

Are ready meals healthy enough?

They can be part of a good diet. Look for ones with protein and vegetables and add fruit, yoghurt or a side of vegetables.

Does the council still do meals on wheels?

Fewer councils run their own service now, but many can point you to local providers.
